 “We want feedback”: Albemarle County School Board members hold another town hall as parents continue to seek answers 
 “We want feedback”: Albemarle County School Board members hold another town hall as parents continue to seek answers By Dakota Griffin Published : Nov. 11, 2026 at 10:36 PM EST Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google ALBEMARLE COUNTY, Va. (WVIR) - Albemarle County School Board members faced questions about mandatory reporting, student discipline and budget decisions Wednesday night as the division continues working to rebuild trust with families.
 The town hall at Monticello High School drew a smaller crowd than previous meetings, but parents continued pressing board members for answers.
 Samuel Miller District representative Bob Beard and School Board Chair Rebecca Berlin, who represents the White Hall District, answered questions throughout the evening.
 “This community has been through so much over the last year. We are still grieving along with you about all the controversy and all the awful things that happened in ACPS,” Beard said.
 Wednesday marked the third community town hall since former Rio District representative Jim Dillenbeck resigned in October after disclosing confidential information. The board has committed to holding weekly meetings to improve communication with families.
 One attendee, Daisy Rojas who is a candidate for the open school board seat, challenged Beard and Berlin on whether they had personally followed proper mandatory reporting procedures, asking whether either had received emails containing information that should have been reported.
 Both said they were unaware of receiving such emails and would make a report if necessary. 
 The questions come after months of scrutiny surrounding Albemarle County Public Schools and its handling of suspected child abuse.
 In October, Deputy Chief Human Resources Officer Brodie Downs, former Title IX coordinator Erin Stone and former Hollymead Elementary School Principal Joe McCauley were arrested on charges related to failing to report suspected child abuse.
 Downs and Stone remain on leave, along with Chief Legal Officer Josiah Black, who was not among those arrested.
 The arrests followed investigations connected to allegations involving former Hollymead Elementary School employee Michael Swiney, who faces 20 felony charges involving seven alleged victims.
 The division also faces a federal lawsuit filed in October accusing school employees of mishandling a separate report of sexual assault involving a student with autism. The lawsuit names Stone, Black and the school board as defendants. Those allegations have not been established in court.
 The Virginia Department of Education has directed an independent review of the division’s policies and practices, including mandatory reporting, human resources procedures and how concerns are handled.
 Beyond the investigations, families raised concerns about previous budget cuts and how the division makes decisions affecting students.
 One topic was the division’s move to 20 minutes of recess.
 An attendee questioned whether that was enough time for students during the school day.
 “No, I don’t think 20 minutes is enough, nearly enough. I think it should be half an hour,” Beard said.
 Berlin explained that schools must meet instructional time requirements for different subjects, which can limit how much time is available for recess.
 She said there have been discussions about extending the school day to allow more time for both instruction and recess, but no decisions have been made.
 The discussion also turned to the division’s finances, including previous cuts to educational programs and uncertainty surrounding future funding.
 Berlin explained that adding funding in one area can mean reducing spending elsewhere. She also said the division is waiting for more information about state funding before making certain budget decisions.
 Board members also discussed the ongoing search for a permanent superintendent.
 Berlin said a community questionnaire will ask families what qualities and experience they want in the next person leading the school division.
 “That will go out in a variety of ways to answer a series of questions about what would you like the next superintendent to be? What qualities would you like this person to be?” Berlin said.
 Listening sessions are expected to begin late November, giving families, employees and other community members opportunities to share their priorities.
 Board members are also planning to introduce 15-minute office hours, allowing families to speak directly with their representatives outside regular school board meetings.
 They’re also asking how parents prefer to receive information from the division.
 “One of the places we’re really interested in hearing from families is how do you like to be communicated? Is it videos? Is it long emails?” Berlin said.
 The school board is scheduled to meet Thursday, Nov. 12, with several significant items on the agenda.
 Acting Superintendent Chandra Hayes is expected to provide an update on a improvement plan focused on compliance, communication and rebuilding public trust.
 The board directed Hayes in October to develop the plan and establish an Office of Compliance and Constituent Services.
 The proposed office is intended to give families and employees another way to raise concerns while strengthening oversight of the division’s policies and procedures.
 Board members will also discuss the Capital Improvement Program, a five-year plan outlining proposed school construction, renovations, maintenance and other facility improvements across Albemarle County.
 The program helps identify which projects need funding and establishes priorities for school facilities over the coming years.
 Thursday’s meeting will also include an update on the superintendent search and the selection of a new school board member to represent the vacant Rio District seat.
 “As members of the school board, we want to listen, we want feedback and we want to know how to make ACPS better,” Beard said.
